slides.title: Ch. 24: Speech Engines
slides.sub: Speech synthesis with pyttsx3, recognition with Whisper, subtitles and downloads with yt-dlp

items.body: Every output on these slides was printed by the Python above when the deck was made, and every picture was saved by a program that is run again to check it. Nothing is heard: the machine has no sound card, so the speech goes to WAV files. Windows, macOS, a microphone, a GPU, a cloud key and YouTube were never used; what could not be run is marked on its slide.

slides.notes: Chapter 23 taught a program to act on the screen. Chapter 24 teaches a program to speak and to listen: pyttsx3 turns text into speech, Whisper turns speech into text, the writers of whisper.utils turn the text into subtitle files, and yt-dlp downloads the audio of a video. The chapter has 17 listings and 1 table, and ends with 7 practice questions and 3 practice programs. This deck follows the chapter in its own order: the engine and its settings, saving speech as a WAV file, the Whisper models and what they hear, the subtitle files, the downloader, and the three practice programs, and it adds what the research found when the chapter's 46 printed statements were replayed. Nothing in the deck is heard. The machine has no sound card, so the console above shows that /dev/snd does not exist, and every program writes its speech to a WAV file that it deletes afterwards. Every output on the slides was printed by Python 3.14.6 with pyttsx3 2.99, openai-whisper 20250625, yt-dlp 2026.8.19 and NumPy 2.5.4, the versions the console above prints, with eSpeak NG 1.51 and ffmpeg 6.1.1 on the path. Windows, macOS, a microphone, a GPU, a cloud key and any download from YouTube were never used. What could not be run is marked NOT EXECUTED on its slide, and what the research measured and this deck does not run again is marked Recorded. Every count and time from one run is a single run on a machine with two cores, and not a benchmark.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.sub: Six parts; every range is a run of slides you can jump to

items.label: true stories: 4 on slides, 2 in the notes
pictures, each saved by a program that is run again

slides.notes: The route has six parts. It starts with what a script can do: the seven uses of the engines, the packages and tools they need, and the pinned release of pyttsx3 against the newest. Then speaking text: say() only queues, the voices, the rate and the volume, the WAV file, and the calls that never return. The third part is recognising speech: the Whisper models and Table 24-1, transcribing a sentence, ffmpeg, and the languages Whisper hears. The fourth is subtitles and downloading: the SRT, VTT and TSV files, the writer options and the time grid, the metadata of a video and the download of its audio. The fifth is practice and the replay: the guessing game that speaks, the 99 bottles of beer, the transcriber loop, and the chapter replayed in four environments. The last part is a one-map summary and the resources. The ranges name the exact slides, so you can return to the part you need. Four of the six stories are on slides and two are told in the notes, each with a link; the seven narrative diagrams of the chapter are drawn from the same specifications as the interactive page. Every output was printed by Python 3.14.6 with pyttsx3 2.99, openai-whisper 20250625 and yt-dlp 2026.8.19, nothing is heard, and what could not be run is marked on its slide.
slides.take: Six parts, from what a script can do to a map.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: The research's two competency questions; the summary comes back to each

items: Which parts of a program that speaks text, saves it as audio, recognises it and writes subtitles can be shown to work, and which can only be shown to fail or be read from documentation, on a machine that has no sound card, no microphone, no GPU, no Windows or macOS and no way to download from YouTube, and how large is the spread between interpreter, model and package releases?

Which printed outputs, programs, version numbers and statements of the chapter differ in current releases of Python, pyttsx3, openai-whisper and yt-dlp, with or without ffmpeg and eSpeak, or in the files and pages it points to, and on what source?

slides.notes: The first question is the spine of the chapter, and the deck answers it slide by slide. On a machine with no sound card, no microphone and no GPU, a program can still list the voices of the engine, change the rate and the volume, save speech as a WAV file, transcribe that file with Whisper, write subtitle files and ask yt-dlp for the metadata of a video, and every one of those can be checked because the result is a file or a number. What cannot be shown to work is the part that needs a person or a service: the sound itself, a microphone, a GPU, Windows and macOS, the cloud services, and any download from YouTube, whose Terms of Service do not allow it. The second question is the watch-out. The chapter's 17 listings hold 45 statements, 46 with the one that was substituted, and the research replayed them as printed. With Python 3.14.6 and the newest packages 34 of the 46 matched the book's output, 42 ran without an exception, 1 raised and 3 were not executed; the pinned set gave 35, 42, 1 and 3, the empty environment 8, 8, 35 and 3, and the set without ffmpeg 32, 38, 5 and 3. The statements that differ are the Voice objects and names, the line Audio saved to that the driver prints, the transcription of hello.wav, the TSV listing and the call of speak(), which no listing defines. Each slide says where a printed line differs and on what evidence. The spread between releases is large too: of the 22 releases of pyttsx3, 8 ran and 9 crashed with a segmentation fault, and Appendix A pins a pyttsx3 that saves a truncated file.
slides.take: Know what can be shown to work and what can only be shown to fail.

items.who: Homer Dudley of Bell Labs, who developed the Voder after his work on the vocoder

slides.notes: Wikipedia's article on speech synthesis says that Homer Dudley developed, after his work on the vocoder, a keyboard-operated voice synthesizer called the Voder (Voice Demonstrator), which he exhibited at the 1939 New York World's Fair. A person played it with keys; nothing in it read text. In this study pyttsx3 2.99 with eSpeak NG 1.51 listed 131 voices, each a Voice object with a name, a gender, an age and a list of languages, and all 131 said Male with the age None, so a voice is a language and a set of rules, not a person. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Speech synthesis' (Homer Dudley, the Voder, the 1939 New York World's Fair), read 2026-10-14; this study's leaves VoiceObjects and PersistentVoice. The use-case diagram lists what a script can do with the engines of the chapter: list the voices of the engine, change the rate of the speech, save speech as a WAV file, transcribe audio with transcribe(), write a subtitle file, read the metadata of a video and download audio with download(). They are independent calls into three libraries, which is why the picture is a set of uses and not a sequence. The console runs under the interpreter of the deck. ffmpeg and espeak-ng are on the path, /dev/snd does not exist, audioop is gone from this Python and wave is not: PEP 594 removed audioop, aifc, sunau, chunk and sndhdr in Python 3.13, and the wave module that pyttsx3 uses stayed. The card records what the research found on 14 October 2026 and this deck does not run again: the chapter page returned 200 with 44,667 bytes and its sha256 equals the digest in the book's own chapter ontology; the online materials are a zip of 91 files, 72 of them Python, and none of them imports whisper or yt_dlp or holds hello.wav, audio.srt or metadata.json. The publisher's book page names the chapter once and Whisper, pyttsx3 and yt-dlp not at all.
slides.take: A script can speak, listen and write subtitles with a few calls.

items.who: Jonathan Duddington, who released Speak in 1995; later the eSpeak NG developers
items.where: RISC OS computers in 1995; Linux with Speak 1.05 under the GPLv2 on 17 February 2006

slides.notes: Wikipedia's article on eSpeak says that in 1995 Jonathan Duddington released the Speak speech synthesizer for RISC OS computers supporting British English, and that on 17 February 2006 Speak 1.05 was released under the GPLv2 license, initially for Linux. Development continued until it was renamed eSpeak, and eSpeak NG continues it. In this study pyttsx3 2.99 started with eSpeak NG 1.51 and saved a WAV, but with only the package the chapter names (espeak 1.48.15) its init raised ValueError for the voice gmw/en, and with neither it raised RuntimeError. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'ESpeak' (Speak of 1995 for RISC OS, Speak 1.05 under the GPLv2 on 17 February 2006), read 2026-10-14; this study's leaves EspeakDependency and LinuxEspeak. The table runs one probe in four interpreters while the deck is checked: Python 3.14.6 with the newest packages, Python 3.12.3 with the pinned pyttsx3 2.98 and openai-whisper 20231117 and NumPy 1.26.4, Python 3.14.6 with ffmpeg taken off the path, and an empty Python 3.14.6. The probe imports the packages, looks for ffmpeg and calls pyttsx3.init(); every row with the packages starts an Engine, the empty Python raises ModuleNotFoundError, and the row without ffmpeg shows the only difference that the probe can see. The chapter's Linux command installs espeak, the old package, and pyttsx3 2.99 needs espeak-ng: the research tried the four combinations on Ubuntu 24.04 and only the two that include espeak-ng started, with 131 voices, a saved WAV file and the library libespeak-ng.so.1. Appendix A pins the 2.98 release of pyttsx3, advises numpy below 2 and the CUDA 11.8 wheels of PyTorch, and says that the automateboringstuff3 package always installs the newest yt-dlp. It names neither ffmpeg nor espeak, and the next slides show what each one is needed for. SAPI5, NSSpeechSynthesizer, AVSpeech, the microphone, the GPU and the cloud services were read from their documentation and never run.
slides.take: Install eSpeak NG and ffmpeg first; the Python packages are not enough.

slides.notes: The sequence diagram is the story of the pin: the reader installs the pinned release of pyttsx3 from PyPI, PyPI delivers pyttsx3 2.98, the reader saves the sentence Hello. How are you doing?, and the engine truncates the file; with pyttsx3 2.99 the same sentence is saved whole. The program runs the same few lines in two interpreters, Python 3.12.3 with pyttsx3 2.98 and Python 3.14.6 with 2.99, and prints the length of the file each wrote: 0.6 and 0.51 seconds for the pinned release, 1.54 and 1.55 for the newest. The sentences are Hello. How are you doing? and One. Two. Three. The research found the cause in the driver: 2.98 writes the file at the first end-of-sentence event, before it adds the samples of that event, and it hands the file to ffmpeg, so a name ending in .mp3 gave a real MP3 file, .ogg a real Ogg file, and with no ffmpeg on the path no file at all, while 2.99 writes a WAV file through the wave module whatever the extension says. The table is the research's record of the releases it tried: of 22 releases of pyttsx3, 8 ran on Python 3.14.6, 9 (2.71 to 2.95) crashed with a segmentation fault and 5 needed macOS; of 13 releases of openai-whisper, 6 ran on Python 3.12.3, 1 had an import error and 6, 20230307 to 20231106, could not be installed there because they require triton 2.0.0; of the 6 last stable yt-dlp releases of 2021 to 2026, 5 ran and 2021.12.27 stopped on the missing imghdr module that Python 3.13 removed. Pinning is not safe by itself: the pinned openai-whisper also needed setuptools below 81 and no build isolation before it would install.
slides.take: A pinned release can be older than the book's own output.

slides.notes: The life of an utterance has three states. The text is in the queue after say(); the utterance has started when runAndWait() fires started-utterance; and it has finished when the engine fires finished-utterance. The program connects both events to a list and shows the three moments. say() returns None at once, no event has fired and isBusy() already reports True, because the text is only in the queue. After setProperty('rate', 300) the rate still reads 200, since a property is applied when runAndWait() processes the queue, and it reads 300 after the call. The events list ends with started-utterance and finished-utterance, in that order. say('') does not raise an error: it returns the text Argument value can't be None or empty. The research also saw that save_to_file('') raised AssertionError, and that with no sound card, which is the case here, runAndWait() returned with exit code 0 although aplay printed an audio open error, so a program that speaks to nobody does not fail. The program of the slide never plays a sound: the engine is asked to speak, the audio device is absent and nothing is heard, which is the local stand-in the slide names.
slides.take: A call that speaks does nothing until runAndWait() runs.

slides.notes: The program lists the voices of eSpeak NG through pyttsx3 2.99: 131 Voice objects, the first of them Afrikaans with the gender Male, the age None and the languages ['af']. All 131 say Male, none has an age, and 8 are English. The voice the engine starts with is gmw/en. The chapter's listing 4 prints the names of Windows voices, David and Zira; no voice here has those names, and the research confirmed that none of the 131 names contains them. The chapter then sets the voice to voices[1].id, which on this engine is sem/am, Amharic, so the program speaks the same sentence with it and saves hello.wav. The research measured 0.89 seconds for that file and 1.54 seconds for the default voice; this deck's own run of the program prints 1.48 seconds for voices[1], and the difference is one more reason to treat a time as a single run. A Voice object is not a string: printing a list of voices shows addresses, one of the statements of the chapter that cannot match its book. SAPI5 and NSSpeechSynthesizer, the drivers of Windows and macOS, were read from their sources and documentation, and were not executed.
slides.take: The voices depend on the engine and the operating system.

items.body: image waves.png made by rateCut_v1_0_0.py
No sound card: nothing is heard, the speech goes to WAV files - a local stand-in for a loudspeaker.
Lines 1 to 104 (imports, helpers and the work folder) are not shown.

slides.notes: The chart is the length in seconds of the same ten-word sentence, The quick brown fox jumps over the yellow lazy dog, at seven rates, each set in a fresh process: 6.46 seconds at rate 50, 5.44 at 100, 3.62 at 150, 2.70 at 200, which is the default, 2.16 at 250, 1.76 at 300 and 1.26 at 400. The rate is the speed in words per minute that the engine is asked for, and the measured speed at the default is about 222 words per minute. The volume is a number from 0 to 1 that scales the samples: the largest sample is 26394 at volume 1.0, 19622 at 0.75, 13024 at 0.5, 2222 at 0.1 and 0 at 0.0, and volume 5 gives 32768, the end of what 16 bits hold, so the sound is clipped and the chapter's advice to keep the volume at or below 1 is not a matter of taste. The picture shows the two files at a common time scale: the slow one, rate 100, is longer than the fast one, rate 300. Each value comes from a separate process because the rate set with setProperty() is only applied when runAndWait() runs, as the previous slide showed. The research set the rate before each of seven files in one process and got the same seven lengths in its run. All of these are single runs.
slides.take: The rate sets the speed, and a volume above 1 only clips.

slides.notes: save_to_file() does not write anything when it is called: the program prints that hello.wav does not exist before runAndWait(), and the file appears when the queue is processed. The file for Hello. How are you doing? has 1 channel, 2 bytes per sample, a rate of 22,050 Hz and 33,948 frames, which is 1.54 seconds and 67,940 bytes, and it is written with the wave module. The chapter says the file can have another extension; pyttsx3 2.99 writes a WAV whatever the name says, so the file hello.mp3 begins with RIFF and WAVE, and the research found that ffprobe called it a wav file. The pinned 2.98, by contrast, handed the file to ffmpeg. The picture is the waveform of hello.wav, saved by the same program: the greater the amplitude the taller the strip, and the pauses between the words are the flat parts. Because the file can be incomplete when runAndWait() returns, the program calls a small helper that waits until the size of the file has not changed for a moment; the next slide shows why. In the research 1,800 words of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland became 450.2 seconds, 7.5 minutes, of audio in about 3 seconds of work, where the chapter says 10 minutes in about 2 seconds; that is one run on this machine.
slides.take: The file is a WAV, and it exists only after runAndWait().

items.body: No sound card: nothing is heard, the speech goes to WAV files - a local stand-in for a loudspeaker. Lines 1 to 104 (imports and helpers) are not shown.
Recorded 14 Oct 2026: in 12 fresh processes a 33-word text was not yet a complete file when the first runAndWait() returned in 8, and a 5-word text in none.

slides.notes: The activity diagram is the safe way to save a sentence: initialise the engine, call save_to_file() with the text and the file name, call runAndWait() to process the queue, and then ask whether the file is complete; if it is, open it with the wave module, and if not, wait until the size of the file is stable and ask again. The program shows the two ways a call does not come back, each in a child process that is given 5 seconds. A runAndWait() with nothing to say, after a property was changed, returns the first time and does not return the second time; and a save_to_file() into a folder that does not exist returns as the first call of a process and does not return after an utterance. The research killed both after 15 seconds. It also found that the file is not always complete when the first runAndWait() returns: in 12 fresh processes that was so in 8 for a text of 33 words and in none for a text of 5 words. A program that opens the file straight away may read half of it, which is why the helper waits for the size to settle. The hanging calls are written here as a warning, and the safest habit is one runAndWait() after all the calls, and a folder that exists.
slides.take: Wait for the file, and never call runAndWait() twice with nothing queued.

Recorded 14 Oct 2026: the columns 'here' are the research's runs on two CPU cores (single runs): 10 words took 1.0, 1.6 and 5.1 s, and 1,800 words (13 minutes) took 40.0, 98.9 and 197.5 s.
NOT EXECUTED here: transcription with medium and turbo (killed at about 6 GB of memory), with large-v3 (3,087,371,615 bytes, does not load) and on a GPU: findings, not successes.

slides.notes: Table 24-1 of the chapter lists five models with a file size, the time to transcribe 10 words and the time for 15 minutes: tiny 74MB, 1.9 s and 1m 20s; base 142MB, 3.0 s and 2m 34s; small 472MB, 9.6 s and 6m 37s; medium 1.5GB, 28.6 s and 20m 17s; large-v3 3GB, 51.9 s and 32m 58s. The table of the slide sets the book beside this machine. The files have 75,572,083 bytes for tiny, 145,262,807 for base, 483,617,219 for small and 3,087,371,615 for large-v3, so the book's sizes are rounded down; the program counts the parameters of the three models that load, 37.2, 71.8 and 240.6 million, and reads the sizes of their files. On two CPU cores the research measured 1.0, 1.6 and 5.1 seconds for the ten words where the table says 1.9, 3.0 and 9.6, and the memory of the process peaked at 972, 1,082 and 2,645 MiB. These are single runs on one machine, not the author's laptop. Loading medium and turbo ended with the kernel's out-of-memory killer, return code -9, on a machine with 8,029 MiB of memory; the README of Whisper lists about 6 GB for turbo and about 10 GB for large. large-v3 could not be loaded under a 6.5 GB address-space limit. These are findings, not successes. The package knows 14 model names, turbo among them. The program asks for device='cuda' and gets RuntimeError, because torch.cuda.is_available() is False; no GPU was used for anything in this deck.
slides.take: Pick the model that fits the memory you have, not the one the table praises.

items.who: OpenAI, which trained Whisper on 680,000 hours of labelled audio-transcript pairs
items.where: Released as open-source software in September 2022; the training data held 117,000 hours in 96 non-English languages

slides.notes: Wikipedia's article on Whisper says it was created by OpenAI and first released as open-source software in September 2022, and that its training dataset consists of 680,000 hours of labeled audio-transcript pairs sourced from the internet, including 117,000 hours in 96 non-English languages. The weights are files that the package downloads on first use. In this study the file of the tiny model had 75,572,083 bytes and that of the base model 145,262,807 bytes, where the chapter's table says 74MB and 142MB, and the large-v3 file had 3,087,371,615 bytes. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Whisper (speech recognition system)' (released in September 2022; 680,000 hours; 117,000 hours in 96 non-English languages), read 2026-10-14; this study's leaves ModelFiles and WhisperPackage. The program speaks the ten-word sentence of the chapter, The quick brown fox jumps over the yellow lazy dog, into fox.wav and transcribes the file with the three models. tiny hears the quick brown fog stump over the yellow laser dog, base the quick round fox dumps over the yellow lazy dog, and small the quick brown fox dumps over the yellow lazy dog. The word error rate, the number of words to change divided by the number of words said, is 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1, which the chart draws. The result is a dictionary with the keys text, segments and language, and each segment has the keys id, seek, start, end, text and tokens. The default of transcribe() may retry with a random temperature, which is why the programs of this deck pass temperature=0.0 wherever the text is printed: the same file gives the same text twice. A word error rate of one sentence is only a count. The research measured 0.1919, 0.1079 and 0.0345 on the 1,800 words read by eSpeak NG, between 0.1636 and 0.3123 for tiny, 0.1524 and 0.2565 for base and 0.0186 and 0.2416 for small on four LibriVox readings of the Gettysburg Address, and it saw tiny transcribe ten seconds of digital silence as the word You. Speech made by a synthesiser is easy and a human voice is not; a transcript is the text of a model and not a copy of what was said.
slides.take: Larger models make fewer mistakes, and every transcript is a model's guess.

Davis built Audrey for single-speaker digit recognition, and that the system located the formants in the power spectrum of each utterance. It knew one speaker and the ten digits. slides.notes: Wikipedia's article on SubRip says the program, developed by Brain and Zuggy for Microsoft Windows, was released on 3 March 2000, and that the SubRip Text file format has the filename extension .srt and the internet media type application/x-subrip. Its blocks are a number, a time range and text. In this study Whisper's SRT writer produced the chapter's 223-byte listing exactly for the two segments the book prints, wrote times with a comma before the milliseconds (01:00:01,500), and its WebVTT writer used a full stop (01:00:01.500). The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'SubRip' (Brain and Zuggy, released 3 March 2000, the extension .srt), read 2026-10-14; this study's leaves SrtListing and ReadBackCues. The program gives the writers of whisper.utils the two segments the chapter prints, a first cue from 0.0 to 5.64 seconds and a second from 5.64 to 14.96, and writes them in three formats. The SRT file has 223 bytes, the WebVTT file 215 and the TSV file 190, and the SRT and VTT files equal the chapter's listings 7 and 8, the research found them equal under the pinned release too. They differ in the shape of the time: SRT counts hours, minutes, seconds and milliseconds with a comma, 00:00:05,640, WebVTT drops the hours and uses a point, 00:05.640, and the TSV file has the columns start, end and text, separated by tabs and counted in milliseconds, where the chapter's listing 9 shows spaces. get_writer() accepts srt, vtt, tsv, txt and json; asking for docx raises KeyError. The picture draws the two cues on a time axis, one bar for each. The W3C specification of WebVTT and the SubRip format are in the resources.

Saved speech and recognition: save_to_file() writes a WAV file, Whisper needs ffmpeg, and the models differ in size and time; slide 12 sets the book's table beside this machine. Subtitle files: the writers make SRT, VTT and TSV files, the times are on a grid of 0.02 seconds, and the word error rate measures accuracy. Downloading videos: yt-dlp downloads audio, the terms of the site limit downloading, and downloaders change with the releases, so 5 of 6 recent yt-dlp releases ran. Practice programs: the guessing game speaks, the song has 99 verses, and the transcriber loop stops at a bad address. Environment and evidence: the study ran Python 3.14.6, Windows and macOS were not executed, and every number is from a single run. Together they answer the first question of the chapter, what can be shown to work without a sound card, a microphone or a GPU and what can only be shown to fail, and the slides that say where a printed line differs answer the second. The map is drawn from the same specification as the interactive page.

A download from YouTube is not allowed, so a public-domain reading stood in for it.

slides.notes: Four claims, each carried by a result you saw printed. If you can say them in your own words and run the examples yourself, you have the chapter. The programs need pyttsx3, openai-whisper and yt-dlp, with eSpeak NG and ffmpeg installed by the package manager of the system, and a work folder they can fill with WAV files. The rows were run again under Python 3.14.6 each time the deck was built, and the programs, and with them the pictures, were run again by the check that compares the slides with the recording. What was not run is marked on its slide: SAPI5, NSSpeechSynthesizer and AVSpeech, a microphone, a GPU, the cloud services, a download from YouTube, and the Whisper models medium, turbo and large-v3. Nothing was ever heard. Every count and time in this deck from a single run is a single run, and not a benchmark. The next chapter of the book moves on, and what this chapter taught about checking what a program writes carries over.
